Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on March 8, 2025
Review Body: I bought three copies of the book to give away over the holidays--and a Kindle edition for me. True story--my next door neighbor, a charming intelligent gentleman over a certain age, got a phone call from his professor daughter. She said, "Dad, there's this book you have to read!" And he was able to say, been there/done that, my neighbor gave it to me for Christmas. It should be required reading--it's beautifully, elegantly written. Crisp prose. Read it, act upon it and your grandchildren will never have to ask you why didn't you and your generation stop this whole sale destruction of American democracy?

Review Body: After reading this book on Kindle, I'm ordering a few copies, one for myself so I can underline quotes from esteemed people, and the rest to pass on to friends and my children. It's a nice synopsis of what happened in Europe in the 1930's through the 1980's, politically. I especially was enlightened by Chapter 18, and the history of how Putin(beloved by our current president ) came to power, and how he demonized the Russian Muslim population in Chechnya, blaming them for terrorist actions that his own secret police carried out. The author never mentions the 2004 election and how before the election the terrorist danger was raised(with no solid facts to back that up), and people voted for Bush out of fear. All in all, this is a great read if you want to connect the dots about what's happening today, and how we're being manipulated to be afraid of "others" that aren't like ourselves.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on September 17, 2019
Review Body:
"History does not repeat, but it does instruct."
Snyder, Timothy. On Tyranny (p. 9). Crown/Archetype. Kindle Edition.

Timothy Snyder digs into the early 20th century rise to power of Nazism and fascism to see if their example might help inform the reader about what is at work in the United States today. He finds compelling and chilling similarities among Hitler, Mussolini, and Trump in their manipulation of the their political systems and their respective supporters. Snyder's writing is cautionary, but it is also instructional,leading the reader through various things to listen and watch for, as well as avoid.

The book is an easy read, and moves along quickly, with chapters that almost seem like bullets. I strongly recommend it to anyone living in the United States under its current regime. Understanding what is at work and responding to it offers, perhaps, the only hope that the country will be able to survive this assault on democracy.

Review Body: There was nothing I liked. The book was written as an indictment of the Trump campaign and presidency. Yet, the name Trump never appears. Data is put forward with no citation of source. Claims of wrong doing; again no sources. It contains nothing of substance and ignores the fact that many of the charges made could easily be levelled against Democrat politicians. He speaks of the "the less popular party" then goes on to say that this party controls the majority of state houses. So much for "less popular." I think I paid about a buck for the Kindle version of the book. I was overcharged. Pure rubbish.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on October 2, 2017
Review Body: This book was like a gift of perfect timing. It is easy to read. Short. Brilliant. Gives you some historic and very important lessons that should be taken to heart. We have a younger generation of Americans who have not been educated about WWII whatsoever- and have no concept of what to look out for. They may even think that our democracy is stable and our institutions protected. I hope they read this book. When I heard Mr Snyder on the Sam Harris podcast I listened to that podcast THREE times-because I liked listening to what he had to say so much. Mr Snyder came across as a compassionate soul who is also brilliant. His credentials make for such a long list, too long for this review. He is a prize to have as a fellow American. Mr Snyder is a historian, a scholar who speaks many languages and has lived in Russia, the Ukraine, etc - and published books in 3 languages. This gem was also on the NYT Best Seller list for nonfiction. While I often use kindle I brought the Paperback and am glad I did. I read it with my husband. If you do not have a photographic memory I recommend the printed copy, plus you may want to share it.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on September 22, 2017
Review Body: This is the very definition of a must-read book. Timothy Snyder has written extensively about twentieth-century tyrannies, in his masterful works of history, "Black Earth" and "Bloodlands." That hard-earned expertise makes him immensely qualified to write this short book about the lessons that we can derive from the ascent of earlier tyrannies—if we are willing to take the time to learn. Given today's deeply troubling rise of authoritarian leaders, including right here in America, we need to learn those lessons and act on them. I listened to the audiobook, then bought the Kindle version, which I read again, highlighting it copiously. That way, I can always have those lessons with me, wherever I go, on my phone. And I sent the paper version of the book to a friend. Reading this supremely important work will take you just about an hour. You won't regret that investment of your time.

Review Body:
This concise plan gives the reader the tools to be better informed and verbally armed to change our current political and world path from limiting free speech, social justices, and equal rights for all of humanity through the basic premise that 'learning from the past can help us not repeat it'.

Yes, one can read "On Tyranny" in under an hour but learning from these lessons takes some time and is well worth the effort. I have to date given 20 copies (hard & kindle) to friends. Professor Snyder has written a modern manifesto for all of us idealistic, somnambulists who thought a better world was truly on the horizon.

One friend has said this is an important book in troubling times. Thank you Professor for writing this. I will only encourage more and more people to learn from your teachings.

This book is a must read for anyone who fears for democracy in America. It gives you concrete actions you can take to strengthen our society in a time when our institutions are under attack. I heard the author on Democracy Now and ordered the book on Kindle right then. I have sent gift copies to friends and also bought the paperback version. Review Body:
If you are concerned about what is happening in our country, this is an absolute must read. My thoughts on this matter were scattered and disordered, all over the floor, like game of 52 card pick up. There are so many angles to everything that is happening and it is hard to get a good grasp on any single thing. But Dr. Snyder has somehow organized all of the thoughts I was having into a nice smooth fan of playing cards. He has done an excellent job of organizing and explaining all of the complexities of our predicament in a concise yet still easily understandable manner.

We intuitively know that things are not normal. This book efficiently and specifically explains things so that you can more articulately discuss the evidence that supports that intuition.

This is initially a quick & easy read. However, you will be thinking about it for long after. I initially listened to the audiobook, then bought the paperback so that I could take notes & highlight, then I bought the kindle version so that I could search more easily.

I cannot recommend this book highly enough.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on March 25, 2017
Review Body: Timothy Snyder was a guest on Real Time last night (March 24). With three panelists AND Bill Maher all talking at once, it was difficult for Snyder to get his thoughts heard; however, there was something intriguing about the little he did get to say. As soon as the show was over (11:00 p.m. here in the east), I downloaded ON TYRANNY to my Kindle and began reading. If I had not gone to bed, I would have been able to finish the book before daylight. His theme is "History can familiarize, and it can warn" and he explains how we can recognize threats of tyranny and avoid what happened after the end of WWI in 1918 and of WWII in 1945 as well as after the fall of Communism in 1989. As he says: "Many of the democracies founded at these junctures failed, in circumstances that in some important respects resemble our own." This should be required reading for anyone who really cares what is happening in the USA today.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on March 5, 2017
Review Body:
This is a short, quick book to read, perhaps 30-45 minutes of your time. And at only $2.99 (on Kindle) you can't afford not to buy it. For those who found his list of 20 points elsewhere on the web for free, don't let that suffice. The book adds commentary to his list, and it's worth the small cost.

For those of you not acquainted with Snyder, he's a historian of Eastern Europe and has written extensively on the turmoil--the killing fields--of Eastern Europe in the 20th century. He knows whereof he speaks.

I will offer you a couple of his thoughts from his concluding remarks. In addressing what he terms "the politics of inevitability," he notes

Until recently, we Americans had convinced ourselves that there was nothing in the future but more of the same. The seemingly distant traumas of fascism, Nazism, and communism seemed to be receding into irrelevance. We allowed ourselves to accept the politics of inevitability, the sense that history could move in only one direction: toward liberal democracy. After communism in eastern Europe came to an end in 1989–91, we imbibed the myth of an “end of history.” In doing so, we lowered our defenses, constrained our imagination, and opened the way for precisely the kinds of regimes we told ourselves could never return.
Snyder, Timothy. On Tyranny: Twenty Lessons from the Twentieth Century (Kindle Locations 765-769). Crown/Archetype. Kindle Edition.

But he then addresses the converse attitude, what he calls "the politics of eternity." About this attitude, he states
In the politics of eternity, the seduction by a mythicized past prevents us from thinking about possible futures. The habit of dwelling on victimhood dulls the impulse of self-correction. Since the nation is defined by its inherent virtue rather than by its future potential, politics becomes a discussion of good and evil rather than a discussion of possible solutions to real problems. Since the crisis is permanent, the sense of emergency is always present; planning for the future seems impossible or even disloyal. How can we even think of reform when the enemy is always at the gate?
Id. at 810-815

In contrast to both of these attitudes, he places history (an encomium with which I could not agree more):
Both of these positions, inevitability and eternity, are antihistorical. The only thing that stands between them is history itself. History allows us to see patterns and make judgments. It sketches for us the structures within which we can seek freedom. It reveals moments, each one of them different, none entirely unique. To understand one moment is to see the possibility of being the cocreator of another. History permits us to be responsible: not for everything, but for something. The Polish poet Czesław Miłosz thought that such a notion of responsibility worked against loneliness and indifference. History gives us the company of those who have done and suffered more than we have.
Id. at 822-827

In his peroration, he exhorts young people especially (although it applies to all of us)

One thing is certain: If young people do not begin to make history, politicians of eternity and inevitability will destroy it. And to make history, young Americans will have to know some.

This is not the end, but a beginning. “The time is out of joint. O cursed spite,/That ever I was born to set it right!” Thus Hamlet. Yet he concludes: “Nay, come, let’s go together.”
Id. at 830-834

Buy this book and read it!
